solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Those who mimic sport said to be funny?

indicators.note: something funny is odd or peculiar, so these letters come out in a strange new order

blocks.note: used as letters

explanation.surface: Impressionists whose game is supposed to be comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny' reads as comic, fitting the mimics, but it means peculiar: the two words before it are the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A parody is a mocking imitation meant to amuse, so people who write parodies are comic imitators by trade.

clue.text: Very quick train’s ending in northern city

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, so only the last one is kept

blocks.note: presto is the musical direction for a very fast tempo
last letter of 'train'

explanation.surface: An express train reaches the end of its line in a city in the North of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Presto is borrowed from music, where it marks a very fast passage. Preston is a city in Lancashire, north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Preston is a Lancashire city, in the part of England people call the North, so it is one example of the category.

clue.text: Model again to get rest?

blocks.note: the prefix re- means again
to model is to pose for an artist or photographer

explanation.surface: An artist's model is asked to sit once more, just to earn a break.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are read in reverse clue order: 'again' supplies the front of the word and 'Model' the back, so 'model again' becomes pose-again.
explanation.definitionFit: Repose is a formal word for rest or relaxation, used both as noun and verb; here it is the noun meaning a restful state.

clue.text: Material in study I am sunk beneath

indicators.note: in a down entry something sunk beneath another thing is written below it, fixing the order of the parts

blocks.note: a den is a private study or workroom
I am contracts to I'm

explanation.surface: Someone slumped at their desk, feeling buried in their own study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it wants to put something inside the study, but it only joins definition to wordplay; the order comes from 'sunk beneath' in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Denim is a sturdy cotton twill fabric, the cloth jeans are made from, so it is a kind of material.

clue.text: Slide and jump not quite to the end

indicators.note: stopping short of the end means the final letter is never reached, so it is dropped

blocks.note: to skip is to jump lightly

explanation.surface: A playground game of sliding and hopping that peters out before the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the last letter of the synonym for jump leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To ski is to glide over snow on long runners, so it is a form of sliding movement.

clue.text: Her dish — Peep’s — potentially?

indicators.note: what something could potentially be is a possible new form, so the letters may be rearranged

blocks.note: used as letters
used as letters, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Speculating what Little Bo Peep would cook for supper.
explanation.walkthrough: Little Bo Peep is the nursery-rhyme shepherdess who lost her sheep, so the whole clue also reads as a description: her dish would be the shepherd's one.
explanation.definitionFit: Shepherd's pie is a British dish of minced lamb topped with mashed potato, fittingly named for a keeper of sheep like Bo Peep.

clue.text: Car — nothing right after its test?

indicators.note: coming after something means being written behind it, which fixes the order

blocks.note: the MOT is the annual roadworthiness test for British vehicles
O looks like zero
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A car that has nothing wrong after its annual inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: MOT (from Ministry of Transport) is the yearly safety test every older car in Britain must pass; 'its' ties the test to the car.
explanation.definitionFit: Motor is informal British English for a car, as in 'nice motor', so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Leaving the job for rail builders to do

definitions.text: the job for rail builders to do

blocks.note: first meaning: an idiom for setting off or departing

blocks.clueFragment: the job for rail builders to do
blocks.note: second meaning: literally laying down railway lines

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests quitting a railway job; really the phrase is read once as an idiom and once literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for heading off shares its wording with the literal work of constructing a railway's lines, which is what builders of rail do.

clue.text: Broadcast across American university

blocks.note: trans- is the Latin prefix meaning across
the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

explanation.surface: A programme aired right across a US campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Across' looks like a container instruction but it simply supplies its Latin prefix, as in transatlantic.
explanation.definitionFit: To broadcast is to send out a signal over the airwaves, the same as to transmit it by radio or television.

clue.text: Dear lover no longer philosophical?

blocks.note: a former partner is an ex
pensive means thoughtful, reflective

explanation.surface: A former sweetheart who has stopped taking things calmly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dear' reads as a term of endearment starting a letter, but here it means costly.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage dear means high in price, so a dear item is a costly one.

clue.text: Poet takes off

indicators.note: something off is wrong or out of kilter, so these letters are put into a different order

blocks.note: used as letters

explanation.surface: A writer of verse departing, or doing impressions of someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes off' reads as a single phrasal verb, but it splits into fodder and signal.
explanation.definitionFit: John Keats was an English Romantic writer of odes such as 'To Autumn', so he is one example of the category.

clue.text: International experiment with something in a box?

blocks.note: a test is a trial or experiment
matches come in a matchbox

explanation.surface: A worldwide scientific trial involving a mysterious boxed item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'International' is a noun here: in British sport an international is a game between national teams, and a Test match is an international game of cricket or rugby.
explanation.definitionFit: A Test match is a full-length game between two national sides, typically in cricket, which is exactly what sports fans call an international.

clue.text: It’s a man wandering over a part of Australia

indicators.note: whatever wanders strays from its path, so these letters drift into a new order
in a down entry one part over another is written above it, which fixes the order

blocks.note: used as letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lone man roaming across the Australian outback.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters sit on top of the final A because this is a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasmania is an island state off the south coast of the mainland, one of the six states making up the country.

clue.text: Homeless girl gets home in Rugby maybe

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is enclosed by the other

blocks.note: rugby is an example of a sport or game
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: A girl without a home finds shelter in the English town of Rugby.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby is also a town in Warwickshire, which the surface uses; 'maybe' signals that the sport is just one example of a game.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamine, from French, is a street urchin girl, a waif living rough; the word later came to describe a boyish charm.

clue.text: Former statesman seen in China’s serious

indicators.note: what is seen in something is visible inside it, so the letters run within the words that follow

blocks.note: letters running through the end of the country and the start of the adjective

explanation.surface: A veteran politician appears on a grave matter involving China.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the apostrophe and read the letters straight across the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamal Abdel Nasser was president of Egypt from 1956 to 1970, a leading Arab politician of the past.

clue.text: Sermon maybe in specific location

blocks.note: first meaning: a formal speech, of which a sermon is one kind
second meaning: the details of where a building or person is found

explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks as if it places the sermon somewhere, but it only joins two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal speech to an audience is called an address, and so are the street and house details pinpointing where someone lives.

clue.text: Small child’s wheeled toy making impact

blocks.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
a trike is a tricycle

explanation.surface: A toddler's tricycle crashing into something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small child' seems to belong together, but 'Small' stands alone as its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A strike is a blow or collision, a hit landing on something, which is what an impact is.

clue.text: Withdrew soldiers given medical attention?

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
a patient who has been seen by a doctor has been treated

explanation.surface: Troops falling back from the front after being patched up by medics.
explanation.walkthrough: RE for the Royal Engineers is a standard crossword source of soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: When an army pulls back from the enemy it is said to have retreated, the military verb for withdrawing.

clue.text: Outcome is not odd when looked at over time

indicators.note: in a down entry one part over another is written above it, which fixes the order

blocks.note: a number that is not odd is even
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A result that seems normal enough once you consider it over the long run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over time' reads as 'eventually', but 'over' is a positional instruction for the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Event can mean a result, as in the phrase 'in the event', meaning as it turned out, so it matches outcome.

clue.text: Approach continuous period at university

blocks.note: a run is an unbroken stretch, as in a run of luck
in British usage a student in residence at a university is 'up'

explanation.surface: Tackling an unbroken spell of term time at college.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'up' at Oxford or Cambridge means studying there; going down means leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: The run-up to something is the period leading to it, and it is also a bowler's or jumper's approach before delivery or take-off.

clue.text: Conservative member has chosen to become a monk

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
an arm is a limb, a member of the body
the elite are the chosen few

explanation.surface: A Tory MP decides to leave politics and enter a monastery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' tempts as a Member of Parliament, but here it means a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: The Carmelites are a Catholic religious order founded on Mount Carmel, so a Carmelite friar is one kind of monk.

clue.text: Regret being impolite, putting daughter out

indicators.note: putting something out means removing it, so one letter is taken away

blocks.note: rude means impolite
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A parent sorry for losing their temper and throwing their daughter out.
explanation.walkthrough: The abbreviation for daughter is removed from the synonym for impolite.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue something is an old-fashioned way of saying you are sorry about it, as in 'rue the day'.

clue.text: Criticise material used for roofing

blocks.note: first meaning: British informal verb for attacking harshly, often in reviews
second meaning: the grey stone split into thin tiles for roofs

explanation.walkthrough: In British newspapers a play that is harshly reviewed is said to be 'slated', which is the sense needed here.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to pan or condemn severely, and the noun is the fine-grained rock split into tiles for covering houses.

clue.text: A wee pest’s destroyed pretty plants

indicators.note: whatever is destroyed is wrecked and broken up, so these letters are reassembled differently

blocks.note: used as letters, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A small garden pest has ruined someone's lovely flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wee' is Scottish for small, which helps the surface read as a gardener's lament.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet peas are climbing garden flowers grown for their scented, pastel blooms, so they are attractive plants.
